method: Complete canonical origin sections were read in their preferred reader edition. The finite candidates recorded below were individually compared against the argument and the complete target paragraphs, with neighboring context where required. Exact contiguous quotations and sufficient faithful translations accompany accepted relations. This ledger records the documented review, not an exhaustive claim that no further illuminating connection exists.

entries.assessment: Read the whole distinction between destructive anger and Isaac’s holy fear, the righteous and upright, and Jacob’s personal refinement followed by the unfinished clarification of his seed. The approved sources explain respectively that collective distinction and how a faculty’s holy root differs from its forbidden or distorted branches. The Tiferet Yosef excerpt includes its practical restriction to permitted reception.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Divrei Soferim explains the distinction between the enduring promise that none of Jacob’s seed will be lost and the unfinished work of making that promise manifest. Jacob’s personal attainment therefore does not remove the need for care within the continuing life of his descendants. This develops the precise reason that Joseph’s turmoil interrupts the tranquility described here.

Approved: Tiferet Yosef takes up the same apparently troubling example of liver and blood. It distinguishes a faculty’s root in Torah from the forms it takes as it branches into ordinary experience. This makes Rav Tzadok’s distinction between holy fear and distorted anger more intelligible. The excerpt retains Tiferet Yosef’s practical conclusion about receiving permitted things; its account of the root does not make the forbidden branches permissible.

Not added at this anchor: Its image of the inclination as visitor and resident is less precise for the paragraph’s specific distinction between Jacob and his seed; the actual collective explanation in Divrei Soferim is selected.
Not added at this anchor: The discussion of Abraham’s fear and the fruit of effort does not explain this paragraph’s question about the liver or the unfinished refinement of Jacob’s descendants.

entries.assessment: Read the complete liver/heart contrast and the movement from guarding eyes to directing them toward the Creator. Two different exact anchors are used: Oral Torah’s guidance explains the heart’s practical awe, while Beit Yaakov explains inquiry from the visible particulars toward their source. Beit Yaakov’s complete surrounding section was read to identify the opening antecedents and the distinction between unconscious restraint and conscious recognition.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains why the heart needs guidance: it contains impulses in both directions, while Oral Torah works out how conduct can follow God’s will. Its account of Torah as a remedy gives practical content to the pure blood and awe described here. The comparison concerns Rav Tzadok’s account of the soul and conduct, with the physiological imagery kept in its original conceptual setting.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:10
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Beit Yaakov explains the movement within the verse that Rav Tzadok uses to redirect the eyes. Visible particulars and opposing powers prompt a question about their common source. Guarding sight can therefore develop into attentive inquiry that leads beyond the visible object to the One who gives it existence. The preceding paragraph identifies Abraham’s observations of sun and moon, supplying the opening antecedent.

Not added at this anchor: Prayer and the settling of blood belong to a different practical sequence; the chosen Oral Torah passage directly explains the heart and the guidance of deeds emphasized here.

Not added at this anchor: Its development of wisdom, immersion, desire and awe is relevant to the wider subject, but its practical mechanism is less immediate at this paragraph’s exact eye/heart anchors than the selected sources.

entries.assessment: Read all the associations of Dan, Tevet and the goat, the joining of Dan with Judah in the sanctuary, and the future circle as hope at the lowest point. Likkutei Maamarim explains transformation through Judah’s repentance; Mei HaShiloach explains the circle through the surrender of superiority before God. These distinct contributions are stated without attributing Pri Tzadik’s tribal mapping to Mei HaShiloach.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:13
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Likkutei Maamarim supplies an inner mechanism for the joining of Dan and Judah: anger is directed through holy judgment, and Judah’s repentance transforms a defect into good. This develops what the architectural partnership signifies in Rav Tzadok’s paragraph. The source explains repentance and judgment; the image of the circle remains the distinctive further step made here in Pri Tzadik.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach explains the circle through the recognition that every person depends upon God. This illuminates why Rav Tzadok can use that image to join the lowest tribe to the highest: their relation is seen from the common divine source. Mei HaShiloach also brings that future recognition into present service through the Shema and the removal of spiritual self-exaltation.
Not added at this anchor: Its actual argument concerns Hallel at the new moon and recognition of miracles; it does not develop the circle or the joining of Dan and Judah.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Second Day of Pesach 1:2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Its treatment of the eighth day, Shabbat and human preparation does not supply the paragraph’s missing explanation of Dan or the circle.

entries.assessment: Read the entire two-heads teaching, the moon’s reception, the heart’s initial faith and the subsequent felt truth associated with Jacob. Divrei Soferim develops the hidden communal root and its disclosure; Sod Yesharim explains faith beyond present comprehension. Their relation is qualified so that the seasonal setting in Sod Yesharim is not presented as the same new-moon identification.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Divrei Soferim unfolds the relation between Jacob and the congregation of Israel that is compressed into the sun and moon imagery here. Jacob represents the hidden common root; the individual hearts receive its disclosed holiness. This explains the paragraph’s transition from a truth held through faith to a truth felt in the heart, while preserving the shared reference to standing before the King.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 21:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Sod Yesharim describes how faith functions when a person reaches the limits of present comprehension. Awareness of providence cultivated in ordinary conditions can continue through an interval whose meaning is not yet perceptible. This develops the initial faith described here before the subsequent illumination of truth. Its setting is a transition between seasons; it is not a separate identification of Jacob with the new moon.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 31:2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: This paragraph poses a question about God’s omniscience and the blood on the doorway; it does not contain the explanation needed to illuminate faith before felt perception here.
Not added at this anchor: The brief servant/son heading does not itself provide a developed argument for the relation between Jacob’s truth and Israel’s faith.

Not added at this anchor: The passage concerns repentance after darkness and heightened joy on return. That is a different movement from this anchor’s initial faith becoming felt awareness; no connection is forced from the shared new-moon language.

entries.assessment: Read the full conclusion: Joseph’s guarded covenant enables the union of truth and faith because a desire-filled heart cannot receive Jacob’s illumination. Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the reciprocal growth of clearing, awe and wisdom; Mei HaShiloach supplies the positive redirection of longing toward knowing God. Each excerpt retains the reasoning that supports its additional contribution.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the relationship as a continuing exchange. A sincere clearing of the heart makes room for illumination; that illumination deepens the capacity for awe and further clearing. This supplies the inner process by which Joseph’s guarding makes Jacob’s truth receivable, and shows why even a small but wholehearted beginning can matter.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach shows the positive direction of the heart’s clearing. Abraham’s dissatisfaction with worldly matters becomes a longing to know their Master, and that longing is answered with clearer Torah and a sense of divine security. This helps explain why the guarded heart in Pri Tzadik is a preparation for illumination: its desire has acquired a different object and purpose.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 47:9
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: The covenant and God’s completion after human effort do not directly explain the blocking effect of desire or the reception of truth at this anchor.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Shemot 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Moses’ truth, Aaron’s patience and the restraint of anger toward Israel illuminate a later anger discussion more precisely than this conclusion about the guarded heart.

entries.assessment: Read the full distinction between rogez and anger, Isaac and Esau, and David’s trembling versus Asa’s anger at the prophet. Kometz explains the moral direction of strength; Mei HaShiloach explains its limited role while evil desire remains. Neither target is treated as commentary on David’s particular historical reaction.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Kometz explains why the name of a faculty does not establish its moral character. Kindness and strength take their character from whom and what they serve. This clarifies the distinction in Pri Tzadik: holy strength checks the inclination under God’s authority, while distorted strength turns against what should be protected. The account of choice also explains why an outward resemblance between two reactions is insufficient to identify them.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach explains the limited purpose and duration of this forceful response. It serves to interrupt a harmful desire, and loses its purpose when such desires disappear. This develops Rav Tzadok’s use of agitation against the inclination as an instrument of restraint. It also prepares for the later Chanukah discussion of a future state in which this struggle is no longer needed.

Not added at this anchor: Its account of Adam’s rebuke establishing ongoing fear concerns confidence that one has fulfilled God’s will, rather than the precise distinction between strength used well and destructive anger.
Not added at this anchor: The preparation of awe for Shabbat’s love illuminates the broader sequence but does not add as much at this paragraph’s contrast between David’s trembling and Asa’s anger.

entries.assessment: Read the complete first-occurrence argument for letters, the ayin following darkness, the goat associations, and the unresolved contrast between Esau’s ayin and Torah’s ayin. This paragraph sets up the explanation in18:3. The actual comparisons recorded here did not illuminate this specific problem sufficiently; the substantive humility and Atika connections are attached to the answer in18:3 instead.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Its detailed account of the lamed and the variable reception of Oral Torah does not explain why ayin can signify both Esau and Torah or the first-occurrence argument here.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Its reading of primordial darkness as gestation is a different creation argument; shared words from Genesis do not supply the missing interpretation of ayin.
Not added at this anchor: This short scriptural heading about concealment and inquiry does not itself give enough explanatory substance for the question at this anchor.

entries.assessment: Read the whole seventy/seven structure, the correspondence of souls, opinions and opposing forces, and the bent ayin as humility and a vehicle for Atika. Divrei Soferim explains why true wisdom produces humility. Tiferet Yosef explains the relation of human service to the source preceding service and retains the surrounding rejection of abandoning effort.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Divrei Soferim explains why humility grows with genuine Torah wisdom. The content of that wisdom is itself the recognition that everything comes from God. This supplies a reason for Rav Tzadok’s claim that the bent, self-effacing ayin receives Torah’s many faces: learning is deepest when it discloses its source and loosens the learner’s claim to independent greatness.

Approved: Tiferet Yosef explains the Atika associated with ayin as the source that precedes a person’s initiative. It preserves a sequence: a person serves to the extent of his capacity, and through that service comes to recognize what was given before his effort. This clarifies how the humility described by Rav Tzadok can accompany serious Torah work. The remainder of Tiferet Yosef explicitly criticizes separating these modes and using the higher source as a reason to abandon service.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Chayei Sarah 1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: The five situations requiring prayer concern uncertainty in practical life; they do not directly explain the humility through which seventy Torah faces are received.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 6:6
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Abraham’s years of clarification and maturation do not explain this paragraph’s numerical and epistemic movement from ayin to Torah.

entries.assessment: Read the complete Chanukah-to-Tevet transition, Oral Torah’s fire, the temporary goatskin garment, and the connection to the Joseph readings. Divrei Soferim supplies the practical strength of Torah in communal learning. Sod Yesharim supplies the exact measured extraction of scholarly force from destructive anger and its eventual cessation when desire is clarified. The inherited source quotation says גדי בשנה where the section opening gives גדי בעולם; the canonical Hebrew is preserved and the discrepancy is identified in the connection provenance.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Divrei Soferim explains why Torah’s fire can be experienced with different strengths. Communal study and the words of a teacher whose learning has already worked upon his own inclination intensify its effect upon the hearer. This gives a concrete form to the consuming fire described in Pri Tzadik and connects that image to the practice of entering the study house.

Approved: Sod Yesharim explains both the temporary borrowing of force and its limit. The element brought into holiness is governed by judgment and serves the work of clarification; the destructive anger left behind loses the good that sustained it. The source then says explicitly that even the measured scholarly response ceases to be needed once desire is clarified. This illuminates why Pri Tzadik describes Jacob’s goatskins as a temporary garment rather than his essential character.
Not added at this anchor: The self-nullification of falling on the face after heavenly fire belongs to a different prayer sequence, not the present account of Torah consuming the inclination.

Not added at this anchor: Its extended contrast between unbounded burning and commanded Torah form would require a different explanatory focus; the chosen source directly explains the intensity of Torah’s fire in the study house.

entries.assessment: Read the complete three-stage Joseph sequence and its relation to Chanukah’s victory, Tevet’s awe, and all Israel’s inclusion in Joseph. Yisrael Kedoshim explains the collective practical holiness of Joseph’s provision; Mei HaShiloach offers its specific further interpretation of the additional prison years. That chronology and judgment are identified as Mei HaShiloach’s account, not silently attributed to Pri Tzadik.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Yisrael Kedoshim explains why feeding and sustaining others completes Joseph’s spiritual role. His power is the root of holiness expressed through practical action, later developed by Joshua in the life of the land. The passage therefore gives content to the move from Joseph’s personal victory over temptation to his sustaining all the tribes: the holiness he preserves becomes provision and action for others.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 3
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach gives an additional account of what the prolonged clarification involves: sensitivity to the suffering produced by needing correction, including the suffering of another person and, as it were, of God. This expands the prison-to-release stage that Pri Tzadik names briefly. The particular explanation of the ten and two years belongs to Mei HaShiloach; it is not asserted to be Rav Tzadok’s own stated chronology or judgment of Joseph here.
Not added at this anchor: David’s radical retrospective repentance and collective repair do not explain the specific Joseph sequence or his becoming a provider here.

Not added at this anchor: Its discussion is about Absalom’s concealed defect and the symbolism of hair. Shared terms about Isaac’s fear and Esau are insufficient to illuminate Joseph’s completed role as provider at this anchor.

Not added at this anchor: The beginning parallels Joseph’s release and provision, but its developed addition concerns the Omer’s purification and the distinction between temporary sustenance and enduring Torah. The more direct practical-life explanation in Yisrael Kedoshim is selected here.

entries.assessment: Read the whole conclusion joining the repair of anger and the covenant, Joseph’s conquest of Esau, God’s watching presence, and Torah’s light against Greece and Edom. Tzidkat HaTzadik explains Torah itself as the purification represented by immersion. Sod Yesharim explains how disciplined giving clarifies reception. Each is anchored to its actual contribution rather than made to repeat the entire concluding chain.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Tzidkat HaTzadik supplies the connection between Torah’s fire and purification of desire that is compressed into the conclusion here. Its preceding discussion develops immersion as a unification of desire, love and awe; it then explains how Torah itself carries out that cleansing. This gives a definite inner meaning to the repair that Rav Tzadok associates with directing the force of agitation against the inclination.

Approved: Sod Yesharim explains how the covenant’s discipline reaches beyond a single act. Bringing the power of giving under God’s will forms the corresponding capacity to receive. This illuminates why Pri Tzadik places covenantal repair within the broader work of governing desire and other powers: a clarified boundary changes the person’s whole relation to what enters and leaves his life.

Not added at this anchor: The full passage opens a further question about the roots of repentance, wisdom and bodily desire. Adding its isolated claim about repentance at this anchor could misrepresent the complete account; the selected Tzidkat passage gives a direct, self-contained explanation of Torah’s purifying work.

entries.assessment: Read the entire opening and both variant assignments, then the complete ois that eventually combines them as preparation and attainment. The approved parallels explain differentiated manifestation within one whole and give a qualified example of differing disciplines. This is an assessment of these passages, not a decision that either Sefer Yetzirah recension is textually superior.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Machshavot Charutz explains how distinct monthly assignments can belong to one shared structure. Each soul contains the whole, while a particular power becomes especially manifest in a corresponding soul, time, and place. That distinction between inclusion and manifestation gives substance to Rav Tzadok’s claim here that the differing accounts can each describe the work appropriate to particular souls.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach supplies a concrete account of differentiated spiritual disciplines. Levi’s withdrawal from uncertainty and Simeon’s more exposed path require different kinds of clarification. This helps explain why differing counsel cannot be evaluated independently of the soul receiving it. The source retains the continuing need to test Simeon’s path, including the example of Zimri, and makes the final higher attainment conditional on future clarification.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Its promise of divine preservation through Jacob’s later clarifications does not explain the differentiated monthly service or the coexistence of the two assignments.

entries.assessment: Read the complete argument about past repair, future resistance, the divine reluctance to destroy creatures, and joy through an upright heart. Tzidkat260 supplies the sustaining relation behind the divine distinction; Mei Vayigash4 supplies actual tests of joy. Its selected reunion passage is distinct from the circle/Shema excerpt already placed at17:3.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the divine side of the distinction through God’s continuing creation and preservation of those creatures. Derisive laughter entails a separation and rejection that cannot describe His present act of sustaining them. This gives a definite reason for the reluctance to rejoice in their destruction that Pri Tzadik states here; the subsequent discussion in Tzidkat reserves a different condition for the future removal of evil.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach makes the clarification of joy concrete through Jacob’s response to his reunion with Joseph. Awareness of mortality, Torah, the Shema, and the immediate contemplation of death test what animates his happiness; its persistence through all four allows him to recognize its source. This develops the requirement of an upright heart here without treating the first pleasant feeling as proof that the work is finished.

Not added at this anchor: Its concealed Written Torah emerging as Oral Torah after the sleep of exile is substantial, but it does not explain this paragraph’s decisive condition of a straight heart for joy; the tested-joy passage is more exact.

entries.assessment: Read the complete question about present laughter, the head-tefillin crown, az and Atika, and the conclusion that wearing tefillin discloses a taste of the future. Both sources explain an actual mechanism: felt life from the hidden root, and divine light clothed in a performed mitzvah. The Sod Purim excerpt concerns tefillin, distinct from18:6’s covenant/giving-receiving excerpt.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Dover Tzedek explains what this anticipated future can mean within present experience: life already given to the heart becomes actively felt, and that awakening brings joy. Its discussion of Shabbat and tefillin supplies the experiential content of attachment to the hidden root. This develops Pri Tzadik’s answer by showing how an otherwise future disclosure can be tasted at a particular moment in this world.

Approved: Sod Yesharim explains how the physical mitzvah can carry the disclosure described here. Tefillin clothe the light of God’s will in a form that becomes accessible through actually performing the commandment. The hidden root is thus received through a concrete act. The complete Purim paragraph keeps this within its requirement of service amid concealment before the unity of the hidden and revealed modes is disclosed.
Not added at this anchor: Its distinction between laughter serving Torah and empty levity is useful in its own setting, but does not explain the tefillin/Atika answer as precisely as Dover4:61.

entries.assessment: Read the whole eye/mind/heart argument, the sages as eyes of the congregation, and the knowledge-to-upright-heart-to-joy sequence. Resisei44 gives the actual function of knowledge as instruction of the heart, and Tiferet Chagigah5 explains joy as awareness that even one’s recognition and giving are divine gifts.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Resisei Layla explains what the joining of mind and heart accomplishes. Knowledge becomes Torah when it directs the heart in accordance with the wisdom it apprehends; Balaam illustrates the separation between knowing a truth and having one’s inner traits formed by it. This makes the sequence in Pri Tzadik intelligible: the knowledge that leads to joy includes the rectification of the heart, beyond intellectual apprehension alone.

Approved: Tiferet Yosef explains why clear knowledge can generate joy in the heart: one recognizes both the received good and the ability to recognize and return it as gifts from God. Its example of wholehearted voluntary giving makes that inward knowledge visible in action. This adds content to Pri Tzadik’s movement from knowledge to an upright and joyful heart, while keeping joy grounded in its divine source.

Not added at this anchor: Its distinction between guarded sight and generosity of heart is a related ethical analysis, but it does not explain the specific mind–heart integration and ensuing joy as directly as the selected Resisei passage.
Not added at this anchor: The sages as the eyes of one enduring congregation concerns continuity between generations of courts, rather than the inward conjunction of wisdom and understanding here.
Not added at this anchor: Its brief white/black-eye symbolism does not provide a sufficient explanation of the knowledge-and-joy sequence.

Not added at this anchor: Its request to recover the felt divine affection shown by the showbread belongs to a different account of knowing the reason for a mitzvah; it does not explain the integration of mind and heart.

entries.assessment: Read the complete conclusion and its relation to both initial recensions. Kometz25 develops the preparatory work of awe and the closely following love/rest. No second school connection was forced at this short concluding anchor.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Kometz HaMinchah explains the relation through preparation for Shabbat. The expansive light of rest is received through earlier work, and the last preparation of awe stands directly beside the love that follows. This develops the conclusion of Pri Tzadik: agitation is the person’s preparatory work, while the joy that follows is the fruit of a heart made ready to receive the light.

Not added at this anchor: Its distinction between human clarification to the limit of one’s power and divine completion explains eating before the fast. That timing problem does not add enough to this conclusion about awe preparing joy.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: The actual tests of joy already have their specific placement at19:2; repeating the same account at this conclusion would add no distinct explanation.

entries.assessment: The complete section was read before selecting this opening anchor. The two accepted comparisons explain respectively how thanksgiving enters the heart in the specific Shabbat setting, and how relinquishing independent desire prepares the opening of the lips in prayer. Neither is presented as a second source for the Chanukah law.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: The Matot teaching explains the inward effectiveness of the thanksgiving described here. In its particular Shabbat setting, spoken thanks can enter the heart and lead to abandoning wrongdoing, opening the very gates of righteousness named in Chanukah 20. This gives the reader a concrete account of how praise and an opened heart can strengthen one another; it does not transfer Shabbat’s special efficacy automatically to every occasion.

Approved: Sod Yesharim supplies an inner act expressed by “open my lips”: the petitioner relinquishes the demand that prayer serve an independent desire. That surrender makes the mouth a vehicle of divine will. It illuminates why the opening in Rav Tzadok’s paragraph concerns the heart and divine kingship, rather than merely the physical ability to speak. Sod Yesharim develops this within the Rosh Hashanah remembrances; it is not an alternative explanation of the Chanukah law.

entries.assessment: The legal height example is read within the section’s covenant, vision, and heart argument. Both accepted targets explain an actual transition from hidden light to human apprehension. The sukkah comparison retains its distinct symbolism.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Resisei Layla explains exactly why the visible height matters. A potential inner purity can still leave a person vulnerable to mixed motives; the lamp’s task is to bring that hidden condition into recognizable illumination. The same twenty-cubit rule thus expresses the transition that Chanukah 20 calls establishing the light in the heart. The symbolic terms Yesod, Netzach, and Hod are retained with their stated distinction between actuality and potential.

Approved: Sod Yesharim gives the twenty-cubit boundary a precise account of the meeting between divine light and human apprehension. Its subject is the sukkah, but its explanation of “the eye does not take it in” illuminates Rav Tzadok’s insistence that the Chanukah light must actually reach the person: the light must be available to become part of lived awareness. The sukkah’s ten-plus-ten symbolism is presented as its own exposition, not attributed to Rav Tzadok’s lamp teaching.

Not added at this anchor: The full paragraph explains finite service and an unlimited divine gift, with the sukkah testing submission after victory. Its broad account of human apprehension is less precise here than Sod Sukkot 91’s explanation of this very height and visibility boundary.

entries.assessment: The paragraph’s actual work is Jacob’s luminous image and the introduction of the pit juxtaposition. Yisrael Kedoshim directly explains the image as truth that corrects Joseph’s religious misconstrual of desire, explicitly according to one Talmudic opinion. No second-school card was forced.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Yisrael Kedoshim explains the moral clarity carried by the luminous image. Joseph could mistakenly construe desire as a mission to recover holiness; Jacob’s quality of truth exposes that mistaken construction. This makes the image in Chanukah 20 an illumination that distinguishes genuine holiness from a persuasive religious justification. The passage explicitly presents its reading according to one Talmudic opinion; that qualification remains in the translation.

Not added at this anchor: The full paragraph explains the surrounding covenant and Egypt symbolism, but the immediately following paragraph gives the exact image and correction of the mistaken desire more directly.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 11:3
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Its Zohar discussion at the same general location concerns David receiving years in which praise can become his own acquired service. It does not explain Joseph seeing Jacob’s image.

Not added at this anchor: The complete passage links Jacob’s throne-image to trust and the eventual repair even of apparently fruitless failure, with required repentance and prayer not to be tested. That is a substantive teaching, but it does not clarify this anchor’s mistaken desire as directly as Yisrael Kedoshim.

Not added at this anchor: Its full argument concerns prayer and revelation corresponding to the soul’s actual need. The illumination language does not establish a sufficiently specific link to the father’s image.

entries.assessment: The preceding account of the brothers’ legal reasoning and the entire two-fault interpretation were read. The retained origin excerpt includes both symbolic faults and Joseph’s repentance. Tzidkat 161 explains fear as a stage of repair requiring further strengthening; Mei Vayeshev exposes the conditional judgment on the brothers’ side. The primary Lublin 1913 witness was inspected for the inherited כדברי שמאי expansion and reads וכד״ש; only the new English attribution is corrected, with evidence in provenance.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Tzidkat HaTzadik reads the same encounter with a snake as more than either injury or escape: the fear itself can accomplish a stage of repair when joined to real repentance. It also insists that the repaired power still needs strengthening. That gives a concrete account of why Joseph can be saved and yet take the event as a demand for inward work. This is the author’s spiritual interpretation, not a license to identify another person’s suffering with a particular fault.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach examines the brothers’ side of the same danger: in the test, a lethal judgment could appear legally justified until a different counsel interrupted it. This deepens the section’s warning that an apparently sound judgment about a brother can require subsequent clarification. Its exceptional use of worldly advice is carefully limited to a test in which Torah’s prohibition has become concealed; the author forbids substituting self-interest for obedience when the prohibition is remembered.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Not added at this anchor: Isaac interprets Abimelech’s resistance as disclosing a defect in love and renews his pursuit of Torah. Although this is a real self-examination mechanism, the accepted Mei Vayeshev passage examines the actual brothers and the same apparent legal permission; a third illustrative trial would add less.

entries.assessment: Both complete accounts of Joseph’s refinement were compared. Miketz 2 preserves his genuine trust and exposes overlooked speech; Mei Miketz explains the purified desire, generous eye, and divinely awakened cry. The origin’s lifelong need for further clarification and help is retained.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Miketz identifies a specific reason why Joseph’s successful resistance did not end his refining: he could still overlook the force of his own speech. The passage expressly preserves Joseph’s trust in God; the extra years expose a subtler flaw rather than proving that the earlier faith and victory were false. Its “two days” refers, in the complete paragraph, to the distorted forms of kindness and strength that produce desire and anger.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Mei HaShiloach explains what the prolonged refinement prepares: a heart freed from grasping desire and a generous recognition that good comes from God. Even the final cry is awakened by God, while becoming the person’s own labor. This illuminates both halves of Rav Tzadok’s conclusion—continued work and the indispensable divine help—without treating deliverance as something a person can demand after one successful test.

entries.assessment: The conclusion was read together with every prior paragraph: Chanukah initiates repair, sight and thought require guarding, and confidence is in God. Tzidkat 190 adds the precise generosity/jealousy dimension of the heart, while Sod Yom Kippur 3 rejects using knowledge of one’s root to dismiss inner work. The distinction between intended cultivation and passing involuntary thought is preserved.

entries.assessment: Read the entire corrected final paragraph through “You shall decree a word, and it shall be established for you”; none of the misattributed old 24:3–6 remainder is part of this review. The accepted sources explain the princes’ independent inward contribution and the divine completion that allows their handiwork to become a dwelling. Nasso 6:1–3 was read in full to retain the larger movement from safeguards, to new Oral Torah, to the joint contribution of the community.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: Nasso explains what the princes contributed through their own initiative: each brought an inward intention that was not exhausted by the identical outward quantities. God then assigned each offering its day. Rav Tzadok explicitly treats this as the power of innovation in Oral Torah. It gives specific content to the origin’s claim that the princes’ dedication demonstrates divine agreement with human wisdom, and connects that dedication to the Sages’ later creative authority.

Approved: Tiferet explains how a sanctuary can arise through human hands while its completion still comes from God. Moses must work, yet the Mishkan stands through divine confirmation; the completed work is then credited to the person. This gives a precise account of the origin’s “indwelling of holiness through the work of the wise builders’ hands.” The rest of the target paragraph applies this to Israel’s purified intention and Moses’ blessing that the Divine Presence dwell in their handiwork.

Not added at this anchor: It connects the first day’s “one” and the princes’ first offering with human service reaching beyond measurable created perception. Its Mishkan example is relevant, but Pekudei 6 gives the more direct account of human action, divine confirmation, and the completed sanctuary required here.

Not added at this anchor: It directly compares the temporary Mishkan with the fixed Temple, but explains that distinction through Moses’ Torah-centered life and David’s fixed place of prayer. It would introduce another organizing contrast without explaining the elders’ creative dedication and God’s agreement as closely as the selected Nasso passage.

Not added at this anchor: Its Chanukah dedication of a sanctuary in each person’s heart depends on covenantal repair and recognition of divine help. This is a useful personal application, but the present paragraph is establishing the authority of the princes’ dedication as the basis for reading their offerings on Chanukah; the selected sources address that argument more exactly.
